newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wages showing slight Q1 increase - HSBC.
newsitem.headline: Australian wages showing slight Q1 increase - HSBC.

text.p: Australian wages growth in enterprise bargaining agreements (EBAs) has probably picked up slightly in the March quarter to around 4.65 percent, the HSBC Markets wages report for May said.

"Our survey of outcomes in federal enterprise agreements in the first quarter suggests that the average increase per employee in the period was higher than in the December quarter," HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards said.
While the rise did not appear to be rapid, partly due to the lack of very large agreements compared to the December quarter, there was little good news for the Reserve Bank, he said.

HSBC said the average outcome of the 26 major agreements, those covering 500 employees or more, in the March quarter was for a wage rise of about four percent per employee, compared with 4.2 percent in the December quarter.

"When we make conservative assumptions about the remaining 700 or so smaller quantifiable agreements, however, the average outcome per employee should come in around 4.65 percent," Edwards said, adding this was 0.2-0.3 percent above December.
The apparent acceleration was entirely in private sector agreements, which were estimated at 4.9 percent in the March quarter from 4.4 percent in December.
Public sector agreements were not expected to have shown much change from the December quarter.

The measure for all current wage agreements at the end of March was also expected to have increased to around 4.8 percent, from 4.6 percent in December, as agreements made before the 1996 hike in wage claims dropped out of calculations, HSBC said.
The smaller number of larger wage deals, which tend to deliver more modest wage rises, this quarter was one factor behind the expected rise in the overall pace of increase.
The 26 agreements in the March quarter covered about 22,800 employees, compared to large agreements covering over 100,000 employees in December.
"In their absence, smaller wage agreements, which tend to pay higher average wage increases, have a greater impact on the overall estimate," HSBC's wages economist Grant Fitzner said.
Edwards said that while there was little evidence in the report to confirm a general acceleration in wages, there was enough to throw serious doubt on the probability of a rate cut.
"Whatever the statistical quirks of this series, there is little in the emerging information for the first quarter to sustain hopes for a fourth rate cut," Edwards said.
